title: Booking schema in PostgreSQL
idea: The schema maps the Java model to tables so PostgreSQL enforces booking rules: one `show_seat` row per seat per show, locked briefly while a hold is written.

analogy.text: A library catalogue with one card per copy. A clerk pulls a card briefly to stamp it "on loan", then files it back.
analogy.breaks: The row lock lasts milliseconds; the HELD status lasts ten minutes.

points: `show_seat` has one row per seat per show; its primary key forbids duplicates.
`CHECK` constraints keep status values legal and require `hold_id` when HELD.
A partial index on `held_until` serves the sweeper that finds expired holds.
Holding locks rows `FOR UPDATE` in seat order, then checks and updates them.

steps.caption: Two customers try to hold overlapping seats at the same moment. A2 is in both requests.
H-A runs `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` and locks A1 then A2, in seat order.
H-B asks for A2 and A3 in the same order. It must wait at A2.
H-A sets its seats to HELD and commits. Its locks are released.
H-B wakes and re-checks A2. It is now HELD, so only A3 matches.
Fewer rows than seats asked means refuse. H-B rolls back and holds nothing.

code.title: Tables and constraints
code.caption: The schema on a real PostgreSQL 18, then four bad writes that the database refuses by itself.

walk.text: Fixed layout: movie, screen and seat. Enums are TEXT with a CHECK.
A show joins movie and screen. The index serves listing shows per screen by time.
`show_seat`: price in minor units, status, and a CHECK requiring `hold_id` when HELD.
Partial index: only HELD rows, ordered by `held_until`, for the expiry sweeper.
`booking` stores money as BIGINT and makes the Idempotency-Key unique.
Seed one show and copy every seat of its screen into `show_seat`.
Each bad write prints the Postgres error code and the constraint that stopped it.

code.title: The hold transaction
code.caption: Two parallel holds race for A2; then a hold expires and the seat is taken over. It uses a trimmed show_seat table so the race stays short.

walk.text: Lock the free or expired rows in seat order with `FOR UPDATE`.
Fewer rows than seats asked means a seat is taken: roll back.
Otherwise mark all seats HELD with a ten-minute deadline and commit.
Confirm books only rows of this hold that are still inside the deadline.
Two clients race in parallel; print how many won, never who.
A4: held, refused at 18:05, taken over at 18:11, late confirm fails.
Final count of seats per status proves the rules held.

pitfalls: Without `ORDER BY seat_no` before `FOR UPDATE`, overlapping holds can deadlock.
Pass `now` as a parameter in tests; `now()` makes expiry tests flaky.
Never trust the application alone; keep `UNIQUE` and `CHECK` as the last guard.

quiz.q: What does hold.mjs print for the parallel race?
quiz.why: The second transaction waits on A2's row lock, re-checks it after the first commits, finds it HELD, and rolls back.

takeaway: Let PostgreSQL row locks and constraints decide who gets the seat.

starters: Why one show_seat row per seat instead of a booked_seats table?
When would optimistic locking with a version column fit better?
How should a background job release expired holds?
